style.vernacular: Dry, sunny Atlantic capital on volcanic Santiago. The Platô has a 19th-century grid of two-storey Portuguese neoclassical buildings in pastel yellow, pink, ochre and white with white pilasters, cornices and hipped terracotta roofs; surrounding neighbourhoods (Palmarejo, Achada) are flat-roofed concrete-block houses in bright paint or bare grey, many unfinished with rebar on the roof; calçada cobble pavements of black basalt and white stone.
style.ornament: Portuguese neoclassical pilasters, moulded cornices and window surrounds picked out in white against pastel walls; calçada pavements in black-and-white basalt wave patterns; iron balconies and railings on Platô buildings; bright murals and painted shopfronts in the suburbs.

sources.what: neoclassical design dominated 1822 to early 20th century, most prominently in Praia and the Platô; many neoclassical buildings had detached roofs; post-independence buildings commonly flat-roofed; pink walls (Palácio do Povo), stucco walls; Presidential Palace and Cathedral survive

Platô redeveloped on a grid plan in the 19th century with grand colonial buildings and mansions; arid climate (about 210 mm rain); Presidential Palace, Cathedral, Albuquerque Square, Estádio da Varzea
Ribeira Grande / Cidade Velha: marble pelourinho, 1495 church, ruined fort and cathedral
